title: Farm near Duivendrecht

image.credit: Art Institute of Chicago, United States; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A farm scene in the countryside, with farm buildings and trees simplified into bold shapes and strong color rather than fine detail.

source.museum: Art Institute of Chicago, United States
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting made in 1916 by Piet Mondrian, a Dutch artist, and now at the Art Institute of Chicago. Duivendrecht is a village near Amsterdam. Mondrian is best known for later abstract paintings of lines and blocks of color, and works like this one show him moving toward simpler forms.

descriptions.k: This is a farm in the country. Can you find the buildings and the trees? The shapes are big and simple. The colors are strong. What shapes do you see? Can you point to one?
descriptions.g12: Piet Mondrian painted this farm near a village in the Netherlands. He did not paint every leaf or brick. He used simple shapes and strong colors. Look for the farm and the trees. What shapes can you find? How does the farm feel?
descriptions.g35: Farm near Duivendrecht was painted by the Dutch artist Piet Mondrian in 1916. Duivendrecht is near Amsterdam. Instead of showing every detail, he simplified the farm and its surroundings into bold shapes and colors. Later, Mondrian became famous for paintings made of straight lines and blocks of color. Look for places where real things have become simple shapes. What do you gain and lose when a picture is simplified?
descriptions.g68: In 1916 Piet Mondrian painted Farm near Duivendrecht, a countryside subject near Amsterdam. The picture is described as Early Modernist because it keeps a recognizable place while simplifying form and color. Mondrian later moved toward complete abstraction, so this painting can be read as a step along that path. Which parts still look like a farm, and which parts feel more like pattern? Why might an artist keep one foot in the real world?
descriptions.g910: Mondrian's Farm near Duivendrecht (1916) is typically placed in the Early Modernist period, when the painter reduced landscapes to simplified forms before moving into the pure abstraction of his later work. The subject remains a farm, yet the artist emphasizes structure, rhythm and color over description. Consider how the composition balances recognizable features with abstraction. What does the painting suggest about the relationship between observing a place and reconstructing it?
descriptions.g1112: Farm near Duivendrecht (1916) sits at a transitional moment in Mondrian's career, between his Dutch landscape tradition and the geometric abstraction for which he is best known. A recognizable farm persists, but form, rhythm and color appear to be organized by internal logic rather than by description alone. Scholars often trace a gradual path from observation to abstraction in his work, though the stages are debated. How does this painting hold both impulses in tension, and what might be lost or gained in either direction?

k.daily: Find the farm. What shapes are the buildings made of?
k.emotion: Does this farm feel calm or busy? What makes you think so?
k.observation: Point to the trees. Can you find one more thing you spot?
k.analysis: What do you see first? What do you see after that?
k.line: Trace a straight line you find in the painting. Where does it go?
k.shape: Which shape do you see the most, a square, a triangle, or something else?
k.color: Which color pops out the most? Where do you see it?
k.texture: The paint was brushed on. How do you think it might feel if you touched it?
k.space: What is near you, and what is far away on this farm?
k.light: Which part of the farm looks lighter? Which part looks darker?
k.meaning: Why might an artist paint a farm with just a few simple shapes?
k.culture: A farm grows food or has animals. What do you know about farms?
k.technique: The painter used oil paint. How would you paint a tree with just a few shapes?
k.personal: If you could visit this farm, what would you want to do first?
k.critical: What would you change to make this farm look more like a photo?

g12.daily: Mondrian made this farm out of simple shapes. Which shapes help you tell that it is a farm?
g12.emotion: What mood do the colors give this place, quiet, strong, or something else?
g12.observation: Name three things you can see in the painting. Where are they?
g12.analysis: How does the painter arrange the buildings and trees so they fit together like a puzzle?
g12.line: Look for straight and curved lines. Which kind do you see more of?
g12.shape: Which shapes are big and which are small? How do they fit together?
g12.color: Which colors are strong and bold? Which are softer and quieter?
g12.texture: Does the painted surface look smooth or bumpy to you? What makes you think so?
g12.space: How can you tell which parts of the farm are in front and which are behind?
g12.light: Which parts of the picture seem to catch the light? How can you tell?
g12.meaning: Mondrian left out many small details. What do you think he wanted us to notice instead?
g12.culture: The Netherlands has many farms and flat countryside. What might it be like to live near this farm?
g12.technique: Mondrian made things simple. What are some things he might have left out of the real farm?
g12.personal: What would you add to this farm if you were the painter?
g12.critical: Which do you like better, a very detailed painting or a simple one? Use this painting to explain.

g35.daily: Where in this painting do you see real farm details turning into bold shapes and colors? Give two examples.
g35.emotion: What feeling does Mondrian create with his choices of color and shape?
g35.observation: Look slowly across the whole canvas. What details can you find that you did not notice at first?
g35.analysis: How are the buildings and trees arranged to create a balanced picture?
g35.line: Which lines are straight and which are curved? How do they work together?
g35.shape: How do Mondrian's simplified shapes make the farm easy to recognize, or hard to recognize?
g35.color: How do the strongest colors in the painting draw your attention?
g35.texture: What can you tell about the way the paint was applied by looking at the surface?
g35.space: How does the painter show that the farm sits in a larger landscape?
g35.light: How does the painting show light even though it simplifies so much?
g35.meaning: Mondrian later made paintings with only lines and blocks of color. What clues about that future do you find here?
g35.culture: This farm is near Amsterdam. What might a Dutch farm show about how people use land?
g35.technique: What happens to a picture when an artist replaces details with big simple shapes?
g35.personal: Think of a place you know well. How would you paint it using only simple shapes and colors?
g35.critical: Mondrian simplifies the farm. Does that make the painting better, worse, or just different? Explain your view.

g68.daily: Which elements of Farm near Duivendrecht still read as a real place, and which have become pattern?
g68.emotion: What mood does the painting create, and how do color and shape produce it?
g68.observation: Study one corner of the canvas closely. What do you find that you missed in the overall view?
g68.analysis: How does Mondrian organize the farm, the trees and the surroundings so the painting feels structured?
g68.line: How do the strongest lines in the picture direct your eye and shape the farm's structure?
g68.shape: How have natural forms like trees been simplified, and how do they relate to the buildings?
g68.color: How does the use of color seem more about structure and rhythm than about copying nature?
g68.texture: What do the paint surface and brushwork suggest about how deliberately the painter built the image?
g68.space: How does the painting handle depth when forms are simplified and outlines are strong?
g68.light: How is light suggested through color contrasts rather than detailed shading?
g68.meaning: If this painting is a step toward abstraction, what might the artist be searching for?
g68.culture: How might a flat, farm-filled landscape like this one around Amsterdam shape an artist's ideas about order and space?
g68.technique: What technical choices make this look like a bridge between realistic landscape and abstract art?
g68.personal: When have you simplified something complicated, such as notes, a map or a drawing? What did you keep, and why?
g68.critical: How could someone argue that this painting is more about a way of seeing than about a farm? Use evidence.

g910.daily: How does Mondrian keep a farm recognizable while giving priority to structure and color?
g910.emotion: How do restraint and boldness together shape the mood of this landscape?
g910.observation: Select a passage where the subject is hardest to read. What visual evidence tells you what it might represent?
g910.analysis: How does the composition balance vertical, horizontal and organic forms to create a stable order?
g910.line: How do the dominant lines build a framework, and what does that anticipate in Mondrian's later work?
g910.shape: How does the reduction of trees and buildings to simplified forms shift the focus from objects to relationships?
g910.color: How does color operate as structure here, rather than as description of local detail?
g910.texture: What does the painted surface reveal about the process and about how much the artist adjusted the image?
g910.space: How does the painting negotiate between spatial depth and a flattened, patterned surface?
g910.light: How are light and shade translated into color relationships instead of gradual modeling?
g910.meaning: What does the shift from observed landscape to simplified form suggest about the artist's ideas of order and truth?
g910.culture: How does the work reflect a Dutch landscape tradition while pointing toward international modernism?
g910.technique: How does simplification as a method change what the painter must decide to include?
g910.personal: What does this painting make you reconsider about the difference between copying a place and interpreting it?
g910.critical: Does a transitional artwork have value on its own, or mainly as evidence of later achievements? Argue from this painting.

g1112.daily: How does Farm near Duivendrecht hold observation and abstraction in tension, and which seems to win?
g1112.emotion: How might the controlled, structured handling of a rural subject produce a mood of calm, tension or detachment, and for whom?
g1112.observation: Which features resist a literal reading, and how might different viewers interpret them?
g1112.analysis: Analyze how the structure of the composition prefigures concerns that dominate Mondrian's later grid-based work.
g1112.line: How might the emphasis on linear structure reflect a search for underlying order beneath natural appearances?
g1112.shape: Evaluate how simplified, near-geometric forms shift the painting from depiction toward construction.
g1112.color: In what ways does color function independently of the natural appearance of a farm, and with what expressive consequences?
g1112.texture: What can be inferred, and what remains uncertain, about the artist's process from the painted surface?
g1112.space: How does the work complicate the traditional landscape idea of a window onto a space?
g1112.light: How does the treatment of light through color contrast differ from atmospheric landscape traditions?
g1112.meaning: Some critics see Mondrian's progress toward abstraction as spiritual, others as formal. How might this painting support either view?
g1112.culture: How might a Dutch painter's relationship to a landscape shaped by human planning inform the move toward structured, ordered forms?
g1112.technique: What methodological questions arise when an artist simplifies a subject in stages rather than abandoning it at once?
g1112.personal: What does this painting suggest about how you balance fidelity to what you see with your own ordering of it?
g1112.critical: What would be lost if we valued this painting only as a step toward Mondrian's famous abstractions?

teacherNote.context: An oil painting from 1916 by the Dutch artist Piet Mondrian, held at the Art Institute of Chicago. It shows a farm near the village of Duivendrecht and is labeled Early Modernist by the source page.
directions: Have students draw a familiar place in three versions: realistic, simplified, and made only from lines and blocks of color.
Ask students to identify which parts of the painting still read as a farm and which parts read as pattern, then discuss where the line falls.
Discuss why an artist might gradually move from realistic to abstract work instead of switching suddenly.
